Divisibility and number theory: source selection and reading audit

Review date: 2026-10-02. Chapter: d_number, Discrete Mathematics Chapter 8, Week 2. This is a documented bounded comparison of eight university-course candidates. Selection is based on this chapter's mathematical coverage, proof clarity, explicit assumptions, algorithm derivations, and usable written materials. It does not assert that all worldwide courses were discovered or that this ranking is globally optimal.

The four principal courses cover complementary requirements. Four is the minimum, not a ceiling. Additional primary courses should be reviewed if a documented gap or future student question requires them. A candidate page is not promoted to “read” merely because a PDF download exists.

Reconciliation and independent additions

  1. Mathematical remainder uses a positive modulus and a nonnegative interval, even for a negative dividend. Language-dependent signed remainders are kept separate.
  2. The greatest positive numerical gcd definition fails at two zeros; the chapter explicitly introduces the computational/divisibility-order convention.
  3. Cambridge positive-input Euclid is extended to signed and zero inputs in the independently authored code; its proof follows exact coefficient identities.
  4. CMU's cancellation rule is proved by dividing the modulus by the gcd; the original-modulus fiber count is retained rather than silently discarding solutions.
  5. Berkeley modular exponentiation is made canonical at exponent zero and modulus one. Loop iterations, arithmetic operations, and bit costs are distinguished.
  6. CMU's generalized CRT statement receives a full two-modulus construction and a prime-power proof of pairwise sufficiency for many moduli.
  7. Euler reduction is restricted to units. Prime-power valuations, transient power tails, and safe nested-exponent reasoning are taught independently with boundary counterexamples.
  8. RSA correctness is proved separately for zero and nonzero coordinates at each prime; no security guarantee or outdated parameter advice is inferred from the course example.
  9. The coin threshold, divisor count/sum derivations, factorial valuations, and additional quadratic boundary problems are original elementary extensions supported by the established divisibility/CRT machinery; they are not described as quotations from the reviewed course passages.

Individual revision, 13 October 2026

The preceding audit is historical. Four independent written courses were freshly reread within the exact scopes in deep-library-revision/d_number-course-recheck.json: MIT printed pages 243–252, all 72 CMU slides, Cambridge physical pages 123–143 and 151–182, and all eight Berkeley Fall 2026 Note 6 pages plus all four Note 7 pages. The eight-candidate comparison was reassessed for chapter fit, complementary proofs and accessible written instruction. Unselected overview/syllabus entries are not counted as full text reading, and no worldwide census or universal best-course ranking is claimed. The inaccessible Berkeley Spring 2022 archive is not misrepresented as a new retrieval. Its earlier exercise attribution remains historical; the new principal course is the accessible Fall 2026 edition, with individual authorship unverified.

Five authentic source items were visually reread on their original pages and checked against unchanged original PDF hashes. Enlarged MS CS 1405 Q125/Q129 crops correct the outer exponent to fifteen and the total to forty. Q129 consequently has ninety-six solutions, ratio six and correct option four. Previous finite checks validated the wrong transcription and do not establish source faithfulness. The correction is recorded independently and also applied to the counting chapters and source producers. The noncoprime-period question explicitly requests the smallest positive period.

The full lesson and all forty tutorials remain. Forty-seven answers now contain full calculations, completeness or maximality arguments, domain qualifications and individual distractor diagnoses. Eight deeper constructions, ten solved transfer challenges and thirty-six detailed final decisions cover exact fibers, generalized CRT sufficiency, nonunit thresholds, prime-power roots, valuations, coefficient obstructions, smallest-representative proofs and algorithm contracts. A source proof using an unreduced value as a smaller residue is explicitly reconciled. Forty-seven fully numeric end-equalities were evaluated separately; a modular residue previously written as an ordinary equality was corrected before delivery.

Forty-one dedicated models contain 216 unique checkpoints and are mounted with the retained exact Euclid and modular-power demonstrations in sixty-one players and seventy-two scenario placements, totaling 356 rendered checkpoints. Small row windows and even-exponent coordinate compression are explicitly labeled, preserve access to the complete recorded data, and retain the target reconstruction. Color fills and mathematical labels teach the actual arithmetic mechanism instead of unrelated magnitude bars. Static diagrams retain five semantic figures, with seven attached Hasse connections and four directed transient-cycle connections. Source/target endpoints, markers, margins, one-line native mathematics and distinct prose/code/math fonts are checked.

Independent checks include 91,880 linear-congruence input triples, 18,496 two-modulus target systems, 46,656 three-modulus target systems, 1,500 zero-root systems, signed Euclid certificates, unit orders and nonunit tail thresholds. These finite oracles complement the written general proofs; they do not certify arbitrary unseen questions. Actual browser checks include 366 control operations, 122 play/pause assertions, scenario selection, eight laboratory records, invalid modulus and missing coefficient input, three viewport widths and print.
